nodes.description: KDF1 and IKK-alpha physically interact in differentiating keratinocytes, and KDF1 recruits the deubiquitinase USP7 to deubiquitinate and so stabilise IKK-alpha. Losing that interaction destabilises IKK-alpha. The genetic argument that this axis is the relevant one is a phenocopy argument of the same shape as the one that implicated KDF1 in the first place: ablating either KDF1 or IKK-alpha in mouse gives similar striking abnormalities of epidermal differentiation. IKK-alpha is independently one of the five TP63-network genes with a human ectodermal phenotype, which is why this node sits inside the network rather than beside it.

nodes.description: KDF1 sits in the TP63 regulatory network that holds the balance between proliferation and differentiation in the epidermis and in the other ectodermal derivatives. Disrupting it shifts the balance towards proliferation and away from differentiation. The network membership is the load-bearing claim: ectodermal knockout of Irf6, Ikk-alpha, Ripk4, stratifin or Kdf1 in mouse gives a strikingly similar phenotype, and three of those five genes already had human ectodermal disease before KDF1 did.

nodes.description: The most consistent feature. Five of the six affected members of the defining Saudi family had lost all their teeth by the time of report, at ages from 16 to 52; the sixth, reported at age 1, had natal teeth rather than established agenesis. Carriers in the Greek family had hypodontia in adulthood. Where the agenesis is complete and isolated the presentation is anodontia without syndromic features, which is a different allelic class.

nodes.description: The allele in the multigenerational Saudi family that defined the disease, segregating with ectodermal dysplasia across three generations. Five of the six affected members had lost all their teeth; the sixth, reported at age 1, had natal teeth. The cDNA change is recorded inconsistently in the sources and this entry does not resolve it. PMID:40463401's Table II writes c.753C>A for all six Shamseldin patients, and that is the string used here because it is the one that can be quoted from a cached reference. The committed OpenScientist report instead gives c.753C>G (p.Phe251Leu), attributing it to ClinVar. The Shamseldin abstract itself names no allele, so neither form can be checked against the primary report from PubMed, and ClinVar was not reachable to adjudicate. Both changes would alter the same TTC codon to a leucine codon, so the protein consequence is probably p.Phe251Leu either way - which matters, because residue 251 is the lower boundary of the amino-acid 251-275 cluster this entry's genotype-phenotype reasoning rests on.
